overview: This record concerns medieval Lithuania, including the grand-ducal centres of Kernavė and Vilnius. It belongs to a world of timber towns, defended hills, workshops and diplomatic letters. Its 1400 map endpoint does not mark the end of the Grand Duchy or of Lithuanian communities.

periods.title: Towns and princely centres
periods.summary: Kernavė was a major medieval settlement with hill forts and specialized craft activity.

periods.title: Diplomacy and religious change
periods.summary: Gediminas wrote from Vilnius in 1323; Jogaila sponsored conversion and a bishopric in 1386 to 1387.

periods.title: Beyond this map interval
periods.summary: The Grand Duchy continued, entering the Polish to Lithuanian Commonwealth through the later Union of Lublin.

sections.title: A wooden town that left detailed traces

items.text: Wet deposits at Kernavė preserved wooden buildings, fences and objects of leather, bark and bone. Much of this material would decay in drier ground. Preservation gives an unusually close view of the thirteenth- and fourteenth-century town.

Excavated yards combined a dwelling with workshops and other working buildings. Jewellers, smiths and bone workers occupied these spaces over generations. Home and workplace could share a fence line, so skilled production belonged inside neighbourhood life.

Split-plank floors and clay ovens survived in Kernavė’s homes and workshops. Ovens provided heat and cooked food. A medieval household needed building skills and fuel before anyone could enjoy a warm room or meal.

Conifer logs and plank roofs formed buildings assembled without nails; expensive forged iron details were rare. The modern open-air houses are research-based reconstructions, not medieval structures that somehow escaped seven centuries of weather.

sections.title: Food, games and the evidence they leave

items.text: Researchers study animal bones from Kernavė to investigate livestock, meals and the relationships people had with dogs and horses. Remains from a princely residence can be compared with town deposits. An elite table should not automatically become everybody’s menu.

An antler pawn only 1.85 centimetres tall came from a peat layer at Vilnius Lower Castle in 1988. The layer dates to the late 1300s or 1400s, crossing this map’s endpoint. Lathe turning helped produce its compact, regular shape.

A taller antler object from the same excavation is interpreted as a possible king or queen. Its identification remains qualified. Even a tiny game piece requires careful comparison before archaeologists can confidently name it.

sections.title: Rulers spoke to a wider world

items.text: Gediminas’s letter of 25 January 1323 invited merchants, farmers, craftspeople and clergy to come to Lithuania. The list shows what a ruler hoped newcomers would contribute. An invitation is evidence of policy, not a count of who actually arrived.

In civitate nostra regia dicta Vilna means “In our royal city called Vilnius.” This Latin phrase is quoted from the 1323 letter by Lithuania’s National Library. It shows diplomatic writing about Vilnius, not the everyday language of every household.

Kernavė’s five hill forts belonged to a larger settlement landscape, including homes, workshops and burial places. Viewing only the defensive hills would miss the people who supplied the settlement with food, goods and skilled work.

In 1386 to 1387, Jogaila promoted Lithuania’s conversion, a bishopric at Vilnius and cathedral construction. These institutional changes did not instantly make everyone’s beliefs identical. A ruler’s religious programme and ordinary practice need separate evidence.

During the 1390 attack on Kernavė, the nomination’s historical account says retreating defenders burned the castle. The old valley town was not rebuilt in the same form. Destruction changed this settlement; it did not extinguish Lithuania.

ending.text: The Grand Duchy continued after 1400. The Union of Lublin in 1569 created a shared commonwealth with Poland, while Lithuanian institutions and communities continued within that arrangement. Kernavė’s local destruction and the atlas’s changing labels must not be mistaken for a national extinction.
